newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Fighting intensifies north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Fighting intensifies north of Kabul.

text.p: Heavy fighting erupted on the front lines north of the Afghan capital Kabul on Sunday morning, but the outcome was far from clear.
"Last night was the heaviest fighting I can remember in the last month," a young man fleeing from his village close to the front line told Reuters on Sunday morning.
The wheel-chair bound young man was being pushed along the road to Kabul by his younger brothers from the Taleban-held village of Shakar Dara, some 16 miles (25 km) north of the capital.
"It was raining rockets in Shakar Dara so I am going to spend two or three days in Kabul with my relatives." he said.

The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP), a private Pakistan-based agency, said the Taleban were attacking forces loyal to former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood in the direction of the village of Kalakan, about 25 km (16 miles) from the capital and Bagram airbase further north.

AIP quoted Taleban officials on Sunday morning as saying that they had broken the opposition front line on the road 20 km (12 miles) north of the Afghan capital to take the village of Mir Batcha Kot and attacked Bagram airbase further north.
Taleban fighters prevented journalists from reaching the front line on Sunday morning to check the reports and would not themselves comment on whether Mir Batcha Kot had fallen to their forces.
There was no information on the outcome of the fighting around Bagram.
The Taleban evacuated at least four bodies from the battle zone near Mir Batcha Kot and loaded them onto the back of pick-up trucks.

Heavy exchanges of artillery and rocket fire were continuing, and an opposition jet bombed Taleban positions close to the front line in mid-morning, sending up huge mushroom-shaped clouds of dust and smoke. There were no immediate reports of casualties from the bombing.

Three weeks ago the northern-based opposition forces, commanded by Masood, a veteran of almost 20 years of conflict in Afghanistan, broke out of their stronghold in the foothills of the Hindu Kush mountains to push towards Kabul.
The opposition now control a salient of territory running south along a valley running from the mountains towards Kabul.
Despite daily artillery and rocket duels and sporadic attacks from both sides, there has been little movement since the opposition advance.

The Taleban, who captured Kabul in September and control at least two-thirds of Afghanistan, want to impose their strict Islamic rule throughout the country, but have failed to quell opposition from various northern ethnic minorities.
